summary
Summary
Participants estimate the sugar content of 32 food items (original judgments, OJ), then see numerical information that differs by group (actual values for the same items, values for other food items, the same values relabeled as longitudes of European cities, or an unrelated text), then recall their original estimates (ROJ) and estimate 32 new food items (NJ). Hindsight effects (ROJ closer to the actual values than OJ) and transfer learning effects (NJ closer than OJ) are compared across groups.

theory
Theory
Knowledge-updating account: hindsight bias is a by-product of adaptive updating of the knowledge base; recalling an initial judgment then means re-judging the object with updated knowledge. The traditional view is anchoring and adjustment (cognitive error).

Key concepts
Hindsight effect: |Δ| smaller for ROJs than OJs. Transfer learning effect: |Δ| smaller for NJs than OJs. Seed facts: actual values presented for a set of objects.
